column1: # SITE-ITEMS-3 curator paragraphs (CURATOR.md rules), 10 Oct 2026 by date -u; from each item's AUDIT.md, NOTES.md head, SELECTION.md row and status.json line only.
# Held: the builder shows them only when data/context_approved exists (created by the orchestrator after reading).

column2: The surviving page of the letter says that something is to be kept secret even from the ministry ('he segredo ate para o ministerio').
column3: The key sheet in the Condes de Linhares papers (ANTT PT/TT/CLNH/0086/11) says each number points to a page, column and word of 'o Diccionario'; we matched it to A New Pocket Dictionary of the Portuguese and English Languages, abridged from Vieyra (London 1809), on which all twelve of the sheet's worked-example groups land on the exact word. Pages 1 and 4 of the letter are not in the item, so its sender, date and subject are not known (the bundle spans 1780-1827), and the sender family's printed edition (Textos Politicos, 1993) has not yet been read.
column4: AUDIT.md section 1 and section 11 (AUD2, 25 Sept 2026) safe sentences; NOTES.md head ('The unit', check-solved verdict); SELECTION.md row 10

column2: Orange's cipher postscript passes Elector August news that the Prince of Spain would marry his father's sister and come to govern the Netherlands, that the Duke of Vendome would recover Navarre by agreement or by war, and Orange's view that, the King of France being so young, it would come to nothing.
column3: The rumours themselves are in print elsewhere; what was not located in print is Orange passing them to August in cipher. The key was recovered by us cryptanalytically (a synthetic control of the same design read at 99.3%), so the reading is offered as a proposal; the WVO editor names the twentieth-century copies in the KHA Collectie Japikse, which we have not seen, as the likeliest place for an earlier decipherment. Japikse's printed edition ends in September 1561.
column4: AUDIT.md 'A2' 53 safe sentence and 'N4 decision (D2)' (witness named); status.json line; SELECTION.md row 5

column2: August tells Orange in confidence that the Emperor has recently, through a formal embassy, asked him to elect his son Maximilian King of the Romans in the Emperor's own lifetime, and that the other Electors will be asked the same.
column3: The Emperor's approach to the Electors is well known; this letter's report of it, sent in cipher, was not located in print. Demandt's regest of the letter (Hessisches Jahrbuch 38, nr. 113) summarises only the clear text, and August's own minute in Dresden, catalogued with a 'Zettel', has not been seen and may carry the enclosure in clear. The key is that of Orange's 1562 cipher, rebuilt from a sibling letter's contemporary decipherment (WVO 74).
column4: AUDIT.md 'A2' 57 safe sentence and unsafe sentence; AUDIT.md summary table (Demandt nr. 113 and 115); status.json line; SELECTION.md row 6

column2: Fox asks Butler to block the channel at Roanoke Island against the ram, and Meigs tells Butler that 4,000 men rather than three regiments are here for Fort Monroe, with 1,000 cavalry horses at the depot.
column3: Both telegrams read at grade H from the surviving War Department cipher book, and a second ledger copy of each is in Huntington mssEC 25. Neither was located in thirteen printed volumes, the Butler and Fox correspondence, the Lincoln Papers or Google Books phrase searches; a blind second reader agreed on 96 percent of tokens.
column4: AUDIT.md '1. Executive verdict' and 'Second audit (adversarial), 24 Sept 2026'; status.json line; SELECTION.md row 12

column2: Kennedy, New York's police superintendent, is told that a man believed to be the chief conspirator of the attempt to burn New York, as described in Monday's Evening Post, is in the Old Capitol Prison, and asked to send on a man to identify him.
column3: The Post report the telegram cites is in print: the Washington Evening Star of 29 Nov 1864 (p.2) quotes 'last evening's N. Y. Post' on Superintendent Kennedy's detectives arresting a man who held the baggage of 'the chief conspirator'. The Official Records (ser. I vol. 43 pt 2) confirm Kennedy as Superintendent of Police in November 1864. The prisoner in the Old Capitol, and this telegram, were not located in print; the four signature code words are unread.
column4: AUDIT.md LS search log (Evening Star 29 Nov p.2, New York Herald 29 Nov p.4) and its E46 row (OR I/43 pt 2); 'AUDIT (LS-V3)' and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-LS-D)'; SELECTION.md row 1

column2: Dana tells Wallace at Baltimore that a rebel agent calling himself Dr Hamilton passed through Elmira going south on Thursday last, six feet two, with light hair, moustache and whiskers and fine teeth, and to catch him.
column3: No printed text of the telegram was located after two independent searches (8 Oct 2026) of the Official Records, the Papers of Ulysses S. Grant (vols 11-12), the correspondents' printed papers and memoirs and the 1864 press through Chronicling America. The press search returned result lists for 'Hamilton rebel agent' whose pages were not read, so whether the agent was caught is not known to us.
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT (LS-V4)' and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-LS-E)'; AUDIT.md LS search log (Chronicling America row, E52); SELECTION.md row 2

column2: Chavigny tells d'Avaux that the dukes and Madame la Landgrave want their troops joined to M. de Longueville and kept under his command even when the armies of the two crowns are together, and that the comte d'Heberstein, who is to succeed, will be gratified to bind him to do better than his predecessor.
column3: About 29 percent of the passage's cipher tokens read, with Tomokiyo's published d'Avaux key (numeral codes at grade H, letter signs uncertain). The King's letter of 9 Nov 1640, printed by Caillet among the Morin-Pons documents (1912), corroborates the content of the Eberstein clause; no prior decipherment of this passage was located in Avenel's Richelieu letters, Bougeant II, Rommel's Geschichte von Hessen VIII or the other editions the audits list.
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT (AUD1-B167)' safe sentence and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-B167)' (Caillet 1912); status.json line; SELECTION.md row 9

column2: At 8.30 PM on 3 Sept 1864 Stanton tells General Peck at New York that his telegram about the rebel plot to seize the Long Island Sound steamers has been received and passed to the Secretary of the Navy, and offers the War Department's help to owners or shippers in guarding or arming their vessels.
column3: Peck's telegram that this answers is printed (Official Records ser. I vol. 43 pt 2 p.21; Official Records of the Navies ser. I vol. 3 p.197), so the plot itself is known; Stanton's reply was not located in those volumes, Internet Archive full text, Google Books or the Huntington's full-text layer (searched 8 Oct 2026). The telegram's frame is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription; the code words carry telegram, rebel, steamers, Secretary of the Navy and the signature.
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT (FV-LS5-B)' and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-LEDGER-2)'; status.json line; SELECTION.md row 4

column2: Manteuffel passes on what the Hanoverian resident Heusch had told him: Oxford had said the Queen of England was too far off to meddle in pacifying the North and would defer to Hanover, while Bolingbroke's declaration had been far more violent (Denmark to be detached from its allies by the spring).
column3: The story is told in the clear text of the postscript; the cipher carries the names (Oxford, Bolingbroke, the Queen, Hanover, Denmark) and one verb, read with Dr Krauske's 1893 manuscript key table. Hanover's own stance, a general peace only, is printed in Klopp XIV pp. 421-422; the report itself was not located in Bolingbroke's Letters and Correspondence, Klopp XIV, Macpherson II, Sbornik RIO 61, Heinsius XIV or Droysen IV.1. Four name codes on the postscript's second half are still owed to the transcription.
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT (V-MANT08)' and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-MANT0391)'; status.json line and grade; SELECTION.md row 7

column2: In cipher Chavigny reports a fear that the Landgravine and the dukes of Luneburg would [verb unread] with the enemy; of the Landgravine he can hardly believe it, given the treaty she has recently made with the King, but he does not say the same of the dukes.
column3: The key verb is unread, so what was feared is not in our reading. Tomokiyo already quotes four words of this passage ('sont mal satisfaits de'); beyond those, no prior decipherment was located in Avenel, Rommel VIII, Charveriat, Bougeant II, the Mercure francois XXIII, Siri VIII or the other sources the three audits list (8-9 Oct 2026), and the Papiers de Richelieu volume for the Empire 1636-1642 was read only in snippet view. About 36 percent of the cipher tokens read; the same letter continues on f.229.
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT 3 f.228 (UNA3-BAL)' safe sentence; status.json line; SELECTION.md row 8

column2: On 26 May 1864 L. C. Turner, for the Secretary of War, warned General Dix at New York of a plot to seize a steamer on the New York-New Orleans run and described three suspects from Havana: Phillips, a Captain Edwards (a Kentuckian formerly in the U.S. Navy) and a Dr Monthny de Lasalle (a Frenchman with a Portuguese passport).
column3: The facts are printed in the Havana consul's dispatch in the Official Records of the Navies, ser. I vol. 21 pp.302-303; this telegram, which passes them to New York, was not located there or in the Huntington's full-text search (searched 9 Oct 2026).
column4: AUDIT.md 'AUDIT (FV-MS18d)' E333 safe sentence and 'AUDIT 2 (AUD2-LEDGER-30)'; status.json line; SELECTION.md row 3
